utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the appearances starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, good morning to my colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic, with our legal assistant Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. Could you please stand up. Could you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Cornish.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: My name is Nicholas Robson and together with my colleagues we represent General Rasim Delic. The Defence has called you as an expert witness today to discussion a report that you have prepared. That report is entitled "General Competence: Leadership, Command, and Control in Contemporary Warfare." Before we turn to the report, I would just like to raise a couple of preliminary issues, if I may. The first thing I would like to say is that both you and I speak the same language; and in answering my questions today, I would ask you to speak slowly and also to pause, if you could, after I have asked the question. That will enable the interpreters to correctly interpret the questions and answers that we both give. The second thing that I wish to raise is: Can I check, do you have a copy of your report and your CV in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have both of them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And those are the only two documents that you have there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the Court's permission, is it all right if the witness has those documents before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there is any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No problem, whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So dealing with some introductory questions: Where do you work at the moment?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I work at Chatham House which is otherwise known as the Royal Institute of International Affairs in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what do you do there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I hold the -- the Carrington. It's a named chair, a professorial appointment. The full title is the Carrington Professor of International Security. That is my title, and my appointment is to he the international security programme at Chatham House.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Could you explain for us briefly what Chatham House is and what it does?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Perhaps not briefly but I'll try. Chatham House is, in many respects, the first of the world's foreign affairs think tanks. It was established in the mid-1920s in the aftermath of the First World War, and the idea was to provide a place where diplomatic and official delegations could talk and, indeed, negotiate in what we today might call offline; that is to say, in the margins or off the record without being held to an official formal declared governmental position. As a result, we have the so-called Chatham House Rule, which is simply another way of saying off the record, and that is essentially the big idea behind Chatham House. We conduct a very great deal of research, policy focussed research, in all aspects of international affairs, covering all major regions of the world as well as functional discipline, such as international economics, international law, environment and energy, and, finally, in my case, international security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You told us that you lead the international security programme. What sort of issues do you deal with during the course of your role?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: We are very involved at the moment in working on issues to do with proliferation and arms control. I'm developing project proposals at the moment on what I call low level proliferation of chemical and nuclear technology and on conventional weapons; that is to say, small arms and the like. As well as that, we work extensively on terrorism-related issues, both UK domestically and internationally. We work, as indeed all security think tanks that are working at the moment, on the current operations specifically in Iraq and Afghanistan. I also work very closely on the relationship between the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union where the use of armed force is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I would like now is turn to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is Defence document D 1034. So perhaps we could bring that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, I was looking when I was going through the report and the CV of the witness - good morning, sir - whether the witness has a predominantly political background or legal background. It's not quite clear from thinks CV. Could you explore this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going touch upon this a little later, but it is appropriate to do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, are you able to answer the Judge's question. Do you have a predominantly political background or a legal background?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Very much predominantly political and non-legal. My legal training is almost non-existent; although, I did undergo standard military legal training at low level, to enable me to undertake duties as a court martial prosecution officer, but that was in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning, then, to the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. How low was the low level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very low.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How low is very low.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the level of -- I have had never had any legal training, so I would imagine it would be undergraduate level, but a very short course simply to enable an officer normally of captain rank to present a prosecution case with very close advice from, as it was then, the British Army legal service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is turn to page 3, first of all, in the report. So if we could move to that page, please, and it is paragraph 4 that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We can see the document on the screens in front of us, but please feel free to refer to the hard copy before you, Dr. Cornish. And in the report, the framework of your report deals with three layers of activity: Leadership, command, and control. You state that each of which is indispensable to military success. What is the basis for you stating that each of those three activities is indispensible to military success?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Simple my understanding and knowledge and experience of these matters, both as a formally a military practitioner having been through training and as a scholar and academic and teacher in aspects of interest here, and, indeed, as someone who has been writing about these sorts of matters for some 25 years. I mean to say that this is how I would present the idea of "generalship," if I were to be, for example, lecturing in this matter to undergraduates or graduates at Cambridge or where ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And are these areas, these activities, leadership, command, and control, are these issues upon which you have lectured --

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- and dealt with during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And perhaps you could briefly tell us where you have lectured about them and in what other capacities you have dealt with these issues?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I have lectured on behalf of King's College London, who hold the -- they hold a teaching contract to the UK Ministry of Defence and they provide the academic presence at the Joint Staff College in the UK. I lectured there, and I have also lectured at the University of Cambridge on international security where one of the courses I ran was on laws of armed conflict, international humanitarian law, and the just war tradition, and so on. I have also lectured in, really, I can't recall them all, but in various places, military academies, here in The Hague in the Clingendael Institute, and various places around the world on these matters. I have also, finally, during my time in the foreign and commonwealth office, I also conducted some close policy research and analysis on these sorts of issues, both command and control and use of armed forces, in various areas to deal with current policy issues in the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned that King's College had a academic presentation at the Joint Staff College in the UK. What is the Joint Staff College?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This is, essentially, the training and education organisation that deals with the transition from junior officership, if I can call it that, which would be, therefore, in the late 1920s and early 1930s, up to the next level and far, far beyond. The idea is that this act is, in a sense, a filtering device to ensure that only those who go forward to higher levels of command in the UK military systems, and, indeed, in foreign military systems because there is a very large foreign presence at the staff college, that that should be a requirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is that an organisation that provides training for the British Army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It is training and education, and the education side of it in all aspects of international affairs and aspects of policy, and indeed strategic studies, that is provided under contract by King's College of the University of London. They provide, if you like, an academic department which is part of the staff college, mainly focussed on training British military officers. I should have explained that the word "joint" refers to the fact that, in the mid-1990s in the UK, and as this happened in various other countries with, if you like, smaller armed forces, all three staff colleges were merged into one. That in military jargon is embodied in the use of the term "joint."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what are the three staff colleges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was the Royal Naval Staff College at Greenwich, the second was the Royal Air Force College at Bracknell, and the third was the Army Staff College at Camberley.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning to two of those activities, command and control, how would you distinguish between military command and control?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I try to explain this in the body of the paper in these terms: Command really is about direction and decision; whereas, control is about the effecting those directions and decisions, and it is, therefore, about the management of the, if you like, whole business, and it's about ensuring that the commander's decision is carried into -- into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, I think we can move on from here to page 5, paragraph 8 of the report, which falls within the section that deals with military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, in paragraph 8, you refer to the British General Sir John Hackett and how he speaks of a military leader being understood as being one part of a greater corporate exercise. Can you explain further to us about the military leader being part of a common undertaking concern or enterprise?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, simply, that certainly in my experience and my scholarship and my analysis leads me to this conclusion that a modern military undertaking is a very complex undertaking; and, of course, as all military undertakings have ever been, it can be a very dangerous and high risk activity. And in that context, perhaps more in the modern world than at any time in military history, there is a requirement for the activity to be that very much of a team undertaking. So I think Hackett, John Hackett, gets to the point very well, which is why I quoted rather extensively from him here, for which I apologise. But I think he gets to the point that there must be a close relationship of a team sort between the leader or commander and those he leads or commands. It isn't simply a matter of directing, saying, Go do this. It has to be much more organic and dynamic than that that is what I am trying to get at, and I think John Hackett expresses it far better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We can move on from military leadership and turn to the next section in your report, which find at page 7, and this deals with military commander. At the top of the page in the preamble, you say that: "The potential commander must be identified as such and must then receive professional training to enable him to carry out his tasks." And then if we go down to paragraph 12, at the very -- in the very last sentence, you say that: "Effective military command should not be expected to occur as if by accident with no proper training or preparation." And my question is: How important is training for a military commander?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think it is enormously, enormously important, and I say that for two reasons. I think no soldier or sailor or airman or whatever could undertake these tasks without undergoing extensive training or as extensive as possible, simply because the idea is that those people are going to be asked to endure a great deal of danger and risk. And in those circumstances, they are going to be asked to do what most human beings would not do. If someone is shooting at you or me, our natural human instinct to get down and undercover or run away. That is what we are wired to do as human beings. Somehow you have to get a soldier trained to the point that he will resist that inclination and will be able to carry out a variety of other tasks and, indeed, expose himself to danger and fire back. So that is the first level. You can't get anywhere in any military organisation without being trained as intensively as you can to be able to undergo those sorts of circumstances. As far as leadership training is concerned, you, the leader or commander, or potential leader and commander, at one level have to be able to convince those you're about to lead into danger that you are competent and that you are able to make good judgments. As I said somewhere in the paper, in fact, that you're able to do the job and you're not some kind of a psychopath or something. So you have to be able to do that to convince your troops. Then there is it another level which is to do with modern conflict, modern militaries, modern armed warfare, which is that it is increasingly a high-tech or high technology and complicated exercise; and, of course, here I'm speaking, by and large, about I guess Western European and the US military experience. But you can see that around the world militaries are, as far as they can and as far as they're budgets can afford, they are embracing the ideas of high technology warfare. In those circumstances, the commander has to be able to, in a sense, to grasp so many different activities and technologies and capabilities that a general if 100 or 150 years ago would never obviously have even contemplated. So it is now a vast management exercise, as well as a matter of, if you like, courage, character, leadership, confidence, and all those tradition military things. It is now more complicated, I would contend, than it ever has been in history.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And within the hierarchy of an army, at what levels should a commander receive training? Is it at all levels or is it more important at certain levels?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would argue that it is important from the very first step, really. If you are -- if you join an army or any armed force at a very low level as a private soldier, then once you have acquired your basic skills, that organisation is then looking to see whether you are able to be stepped up to the next level, because, in a sense, what they want to do is, not only confirm that you can do the basic military job, but that you can then lead others in doing the basic military job. So at any level in any organisation, whether it be army, navy, or air force, or anything else you can think of, and I would say in any country, there is the idea that actually party of being - let me use the term, "a soldier," but I mean it to include everything - part of being a soldier is not simply being able to act as a soldier and do the basic military things, but also to gradually acquire the skills of command. Now, I think this becomes very important because what it then means is that ideally, as a person rises to the top of the - I call it here the command chain - or if you like the system or the hierarchy, it should mean that that person will have acquired, by the time he gets to, let's say, a brigadier, he will have acquired, or she, an enormous level of experience at every single level of command. So that is, essentially, the way it should go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what is the likely result if a commander lacks training, if you're able to say?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, there have been, I guess, examples in history - I don't have them at hand - where a commander proves to be unable to cope with a level of command into which he is thrust. I think this is sometimes known as the "Peter Principle," whereby your level of incompetence is only revealed once you're promoted into it. So this, as it were, incompetent officer might find himself running something which is simply beyond his training or his understanding. I'm having some difficulty with this because in my limited experience, this is simply not something that should happen. It should be the case that this person will have gone through all the levels of training and so forth, and, unless he was asleep, would have understood the basic ideas and should, therefore, have some level of competence. The importance, I guess, is that promotions, of course, always can happen, as it termed, in the field, in the midst of combat. And there you can often find a very junior officer, let's say a lieutenant-colonel in his late 20s and the equivalence in other armed services, being promoted very, very highly to command, let's say, a brigade or even a division. Clearly, in the midst of a war, he won't have been able to attend staff college and so on. But in those circumstances, it will have been his performance in combat that will have earned him the reputation and, therefore, as it were, qualified him for promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Still, on the same topic, you've just explained to us about members of an army rising up through the system or the hierarchy. How does a commander normally move up through the military hierarchy; in other words, how is he normally assigned to a new position?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, a position would become -- I can only speak here really of my understanding of just one system, which, of course, is the British system, whereby, in a sense, you have a body of people moving up, you know, a ever narrowing hierarchy; and people fall off at the top, as they retire, or worse, in time of war, and, therefore, they create a vacancy, which is then to be filled by the juniors. And at each level, there is a discussion as to which of those juniors should fill those posts, which is best qualified, and then extensive review of reports and all that kind of thing to make the judgment about how should be promoted. I suppose what I am trying to say is that in normal peacetime circumstances, it is not something that happens arbitrarily. It should happen as a result of a very long process, which, in a sense, has been going on for years and years. From a very junior level, military officers are being gauged, being assessed for their likely level, top level of command: Could this person become a lieutenant-colonel, commanding a battalion or could he go even further?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. You said that in peacetime there is a process which is a complex one; but in wartime, there are occasions when decisions have to be made urgently, decisions that would not take into account all the data. To a point, would there be situations where not everything would not be taken into account to nominate, appoint a commander, in your country, of course, because you were talking about your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that circumstance, I would say that the promotion might happen as follows; in that a more senior officer requiring a promotion below him, a vacancy occurring below him, would have within his scope of commander the ability to promote within his command someone up to the new level. So if you are a general and you need a new brigadier below you, then you would look him, below that level, to find someone within your command structure who you think, on the basis of that person's performance in combat, could do the job. You're absolutely right, Madam. Of course, there would be no opportunity or little opportunity to read confidential reports going back for 25 years and all that sort of stuff. He would have to make an instant judgment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just following on from that, in such a situation, could you tell us a little bit about the process by which an officer would be assigned to a new commander position. In your experience, how would you expect it to occur?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Forgive me for asking, do you mean in times of peace or in times of conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, first of all, in times of peace, if we could consider that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then it would be known, for example, that such-and-such an appointment would be coming up in two and a half years or three years time, and that the candidates for that position would know who they are, because of course they're all ambitious men and women. There would be a number of people who would want that post, and they would either have put themselves forward for it or they would have been told that they are being nominated for it. So there would then be a selection process, and I guess, I don't know, a year or so in advance, or whatever, somebody would be told that it was be their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then, turning to the next question: How about in a time of war, what sort of process would be involved in a commander taking over new role?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: The idea here would be to make it as detailed and as extensive as you possibly can, and I guess that in times of conflict, that's a rate limiting factor. So you have to imagine that a commander might be told, "You are to take over because someone has been injured or worse than that and you are to take over instantly." That person would, therefore, have to do that, and the unit or organisation he was taking over would have to be trained and organised to accept a new commander, and the whole thing would have to work that way. If there was some possibility of doing it "properly ," then it might run as follows: The candidate or the new commander would be told that it with as to be his post. He would then have what is known in military circles as a period of "handover, takeover." So the incumbent would meet the new candidate or his replacement. They would go through as long as discussion as they could about the nature of the command. The new commander would go and visit the ground for which he was responsible. He would go and visit his sub-unit commander. He would require briefings from his sub-unit commanders. And he would, essentially, look into As much of his new command a he could before or, more or less, at the time at which he was taking over. So it gives him a chance to find out exactly what he is going into, and it also gives him a chance to -- to impose his personal presence and his personal authority over the new command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what sort of period of time could that process take whereby the new commander imposes his personal presence over the new command structure?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would say it could take anything, really, from minutes, in time of immediate urgent conflict, to several days really, because particularly if the handover, takeover is at very high level, then there is, quite clearly, so much more to see and to understand. So the new commander would have an awful lot more to -- to visit and to see and to be briefed upon. So this, I guess, could take several days, I don't know, perhaps even as long as a week. That is, as I describe it, the proper way of doing things. It might be a bit of a luxury, but that would be the way you would seek to achieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Turning to page 9, paragraph 17 of your report, you deal with some concepts here, and the first one I wish to discuss with you is unity of command. Can you explain for us what this concept entails?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It is quite simple, really. It's the idea that there should be only one person ultimately in charge, one person making the discussion, one person responsible for making that decision, therefore, and deciding how the operation at whatever level is to be run. If there were to be two or more people making decisions, then I guess it might work if those decisions were identical; but if they are identical, then it is superfluous to have more than one. But the real danger is that if have you more than one person in command, you might end up with orders which conflict, and these are orders which are to go to subordinate units or formations. And if a subordinate unit or formation commander receives two orders which conflict, then he has, or she, might have no idea which one to follow. So there's confusion. So the idea is that you should avoid that at all costs in a military system through this idea of unity of commander. Napoleon Bonaparte at once said that it was be better to have one bad general than two good ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you explain what is the basis of this concept, the unity of command? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It's difficult to track it down. I'm not sure I could find the precise source of it. It is one of these ideas, one of these concepts that is really, I think, considered so -- so basic and so obvious to the military system, if you like, that's it has -- it no more has a clear source than the idea of tactics, of actually fighting the enemy. I mean, that is the idea. That is what you're supposed to do, but there is no clear definitive source for that idea. I think it is as old as it possibly can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. Moving, then, to the other concept that you mention in this paragraph, chain of command. Can you explain for us what you mean by chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think, for my understanding, unity of command is more conceptual; chain of command is more descriptive. The term "chain of command" describes the way things should be if you are operating according to the principle of unity of command; that is to say, there becomes -- as I think I said earlier, it is useful to think in terms of a pyramidal hierarchical structure, with one man or woman at the top giving orders to three or four below him or her and on you go. The idea is that wherever you are in that system, you must know who is subordinate to you and to whom you are subordinate, in order that there can be several chains of command within the system but, ultimately, it conforms to one major chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just touching on what you've told us, within paragraph 17, you say that: "The arrangement of a military hierarchy would be explicit and predesignated." Typically, how would this be done in an army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, let me start from the top. A divisional commander, let's say this is division number 1, would have under command three brigades, A, B, and C; and each of those brigades would have under their command three battalions, A1, A2, and A3, and so on. The point is that, at each level, each commander, each unit, the whole thing, would know where they fit into the system. So battalion A3 would know that it is part of brigade A and part of division 1. It is, again n my experience, but I don't think this is a peculiar experience, it is a very well understood and actually very important part of the military system to know where you fit into the overall scheme of things, and it is often used actually to generate sub-unit pride and loyalty and so on. So you would find, for example, that the units of a brigade would consider themselves better than the units of another brigade for no other reason than that they belonged to that brigade. But that is all the idea of introducing a competitive and improving spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I see. So you say that units would know where they would fit into the overall scheme of things. In your report, you say that assignments to chain of command can be altered as operations progress. Could you tell us by what process would a unit normally be assigned to a different part of the chain of command, if that was to be done?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yeah, as it can happen. But, of course, no military commander would say that that this is the only it can ever happen, because at the most senior level that person who is in charge has beneath him a vast set of resources. His job is to use those resources in order to meet his task, to prevent defeat or whatever you like. So what he must do is look at those resources and use them as best he thinks he should. Now, if the standard hierarchy, the standard arrangement that I have been talking about, if that looks to be fit for the task, able to achieve the goal, then the commander will simply make use of it as it stands. If, however, he thinks that there needs to be some re-arrangement to take account of new circumstances or unforeseen challenges, then he must make those changes, otherwise he would be an idiot. He would have to redeploy forces; for example, if, at some point in his front line, one commander far down the command chain was receiving more pressure than another one further over here, then he would have to make a movement in order to seal that gap, so to speak. The way he would do that would be by making use of the command chain but not by going around it. So he would say, if he is, let's say, a very senior army corps commander, he would say to the commander of division number 1, "I need you to provide some assistance to the commander of division number 2" and the commander of division number 1 says, "Fine," And he then says to one of his brigade commanders, "I need to you provide me with one battalion that I can then give to commander of division number 2." So all the way down the command chain, it is understood that this is a direction through the command chain to provide a reinforcement to somewhere else in the system. So there is, in a sense, no argument. It is a well understood military practice, but it has to be done properly and deliberately and carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In connection with this, in your report, you say that alterations to the chain of command are only ever undertaken after careful deliberation and with careful planning. What steps, if any, would be taken when altering the chain of command and moving when you need to another?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It would be iterative. It would be a matter of a senior commander receiving either the order or the request to help, and he would then look to his subordinate commanders and say, "This is what I have to do, and I need a battalion," or whatever it might be. I'm using just one limited example, of course. But the idea is that a battalion is needed, he would then ask his various brigade commanders for one battalion. One brigade might, I don't know, let's say, they might be exhausted having just been fighting. Another one might say, "We have only just received lots of very new troops and they're not very experienced." The third one might say, "Well, we have actually just been resting, so we're in very good shape. So you can have one of mine," and so he provides it. It is all done by, as I said an iterative. It is a dialogue. In a sense, there is no doubt that at some point a battalion will be provided, but it is it as reasonably -- as reasonable a dialogue you can except in the circumstances to ensure that the right battalion is moved. After all, I'm sorry just to label this, that commander wants to ensure that what is left under his command is also in good shape. So he wants to make sure that he can protect his own force as well and that the whole thing will be sustainable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. So to use your example, if a battalion under one brigade was moved across so that it then came under a different brigade, who would control the battalion after the change, after the alteration?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: There would be absolutely no doubt whatsoever, and there could be no doubt whatsoever, that there would be a change of command. This would be critical, and the battalion commander would know that, that he would be going out of one command structure into another. There should be actually no gap between the two, and you see it written in terms of a timing, you know: At 7.00 on the 15th of April, you cease to be under command of brigade A, and you will command the commander of brigade B. It is as clear as that. So one minute to the next, there would be a transition of command. If you don't have that, then, again, you have no unity of command, because that battalion commander is then in a position of not knowing where he's going to be receiving his orders from and to whom he should give his information. So it is absolutely critical that one command chain ends as another one begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So at the precise moment in time, the battalion commander will no longer receive instructions from and report to brigade commander A [Realtime transcript read in error "commander B"]; but at that moment, he will receive instructions from brigade commander B, and he will begin to report to that new brigade commander. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. In my understanding, that would be absolutely fundamental.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And for what sort of time-period could this alteration last for? Would it be permanent or would it be for a particular period of time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It could be anything, really. It could be -- it could well be permanent. As I said, the senior commander has the right to reorganise and redeploy his forces as he -- in a sense, as he sees fit. But for the sake of the coherence and consistency of the organisation overall, you would probably expect or hope that that detached unit would go for a few hours or a few days and would then come back again to restore the coherence and fitness of the organisation it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to correct one matter in the transcript. At page 21, at line 16, it states, in connection with the battalion commander, that "he will no longer receive instructions from and report to brigade 'commander B'; but at that moment, he will receive instructions from brigade 'commander B.'" It should, of course, say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Commander A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, he will receive instructions from brigade commander A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're on this point, now that we have had a little bit pause to correct the transcript. Sir, you were saying there should be careful deliberation and careful planing. Who deliberates before these changes in command structure take place? I'm getting a little confused because I thought you said there should be one commander and the commander gives instructions. Now there is a question of deliberation. Who deliberates with who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there is no doubt that a decision has been made. In the example that we're using, a battalion is to be moved from one area to another. So it is going to happen. The deliberation would take place between the senior commander and his more junior commanders. One of them might say, "Well, I can't send any of my battalions because they are all untrained or exhausted or whatever." So in the end, it would come back to one of other battalion commanders who would then provide the battalion that would then be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you are saying, in fact, that, as the commander gives the command, say, a corps commander gives a command to the brigade, to say, "I want you to give a battalion to brigade B," the commander of the brigade has the right to talk back and say, "Sorry. I can't give you that. My guys are tired. They have just been working."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there would be. You would expect that they would all be -- as I said, it all has to happen, but what they want to have transferred is a battalion that is able to do the new job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be no point that transferring one of his under strength or exhausted or whatever. So there would be an exchange of information in order to identify the most suitable solution, but there would have to be a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: With the example that you have given us, if a battalion was to be moved across the chain of command, at which -- which level would take the decision to move the battalion ordinarily?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say. It would -- it would obviously have to happen beyond the level of brigade because we're talking about taking a battalion outside of the existing command chain, and that battalion answers to a brigade headquarters. So it could happen at the level beyond the brigade which is the division, or it could happen beyond the level beyond the division which is the corps or whatever you use. So it would -- it could happen at the level at which the problem, in a sense, is identified and at which a senior officer decides that there is to be a certain action to rectify the problem. That decision then goes back down the chain of command until a solution found which is then provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. Could you tell us what would be the likely result if, after a change in the chain of command, the unit did not report to the new commander but continued to report to the former commander?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This would -- I think I would put it as strongly as saying that this would be military anathema, because this would breach the basic fundamental idea of unity of command, and it would undermine the system of the command chain. So that would be the first fairly major problem. The second problem would be -- could be more practical, in that -- and it is to do with what the military call operational security. What that means is that everybody in this complicated system should know what everybody else is doing. And if, to go back to our example, you are a battalion commander and you have no idea of what the neighbouring battalion commander is doing, or indeed who this person is or who he is taking orders from, then this is an very grave danger that you might misinterpret his actions, you might see some of troops where you think they shouldn't be, you might think they are enemy forces, you might fire on them, and so on. So there has to be a very, very close understanding of what the disposition of forces is and what the tasks are that they are undertaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, moving to a slightly different issue within chain of command and unity of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, this is a crucial point. Could you explore with the witness how is information ensured between battalions who fight next door, so to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an issue I'm going to explore because it is dealt with in the report. So, perhaps, if you allow me, I will come to that. And if you have any further questions, you can obviously let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So dealing with unity of command, and putting the issue slightly differently, what if there's a situation where, within a military unit, there are a number of individuals who all purport to the commander of the unit, and it is not clear to the superior commander at the next level up who has ultimate authority over that unit, what are the likely problems, if any, that could arise?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would say in the very unlikely circumstance that there would be -- again, I find this difficult to conceive of. It sort of contradicts all of my understanding and experience. But let's suppose that there were such a circumstance of three or four people saying that they were in charge, then that organisation, it seems to me, would be close to being entirely dysfunctional. Going back to one of my first remarks, that, in the end, a military system, particularly a military system because of the dangers and urgency and so on, has to have a decision coming by some means to enable the organisation to function. You would have three or four different. Again, if they were at all the same decisions, then fine, but superfluous. But if they were different decisions, then that organisation, I would say, could not possibly function effectively. This isn't simply three or four people sitting around a table discussing the way the world looks. They are actually running something. It might not be military, it could be a business, it could be anything. If those instructions or ideas conflict with each other, then I, forgive me, but I don't see how that organisation could be said to be effective or could actually run very well at all. As far as that organisation's superior is concerned, then, again, I think you would repeat the confusion in a way, because, let's say going back to our example, the brigade commander would not know to whom he or she should be giving orders and receiving information. He would also look at an organisation that was, in military terms, dysfunctional; and he would say to himself or herself, "How can I trust this organisation, how can I give it a task, if it is organised in the way it appears to be?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So it is important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I just interrupt. What was the question? If you look at page 25, line 10, is it individuals who all purport to be the commander or who all the report to the commander? There's been some correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Purport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Purport to be the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Dr. Cornish, does it follow, then, that it is important for a superior commander to know who was in command of a subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is very important, because I think everything I've read and understood about these matters suggests to me that -- that a personal command relationship builds up between a senior commander and his subordinate commanders, and between them and their subordinates, because they have to know that that person is able to take on the pressures of command and all of the things that I have been talking. They have to, more to the point, they have to be in a position whereby they can trust that commander to carry out the orders or instructions that have been given. So there must be a big personal dimension to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Still on the issue of military commander, I'm going to move on to a slightly different topic, and this is on page 10 at paragraph 21, and this is a paragraph which deals with soldiers joining a military organisation. And in the middle of the paragraph, you say: "The soldiers initial act of consent to be led is characteristically and largely non-reversible. Can you explain why this is the case?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This refers, obviously, to voluntarily armed forces primarily, but I would say not exclusively. In a sense, you could argue that where armed forces are conscripted, where there is compulsory military service, in a sense - I wouldn't want to push this point to far - there is an assumed consent which is being employed. But the main point I'm making here is that this person has to make a decision to join an armed force; and once he or she makes that decision, it is inconceivable that what they are joining is something that cannot allow that decision to be changed next month or when things change or because "I wanted to go on a longer holiday that than you're going to give me" or whatever. It is a very serious undertaking which has to be made. The British strategist Lidell Hart referred to the idea of an unlimited liability. I mean, that is taking it too far, but there is something of the idea in that. You're joining something and you're making a serious commitment for a number of years which you cannot break. Of course, we all undertake contracts of various sorts which we might change our minds about and, actually, in effect, we might decide to break. And in the military, you can break your contract, but you can only do so through a very deliberate process. You apply for resignation and so on and so forth. I would say it would be very rare for that to happen during time of conflict, because the thing would simply fall apart. So, at risk of repeating myself, when this person signs up, he or she signs up to an organisation which then expects them to remain there in position for the agreed time, whether it be two years or three or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what sort of problems could arise if a soldier was able to unilaterally terminate his relationship with the army and leave at any stage, if you are able to say?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would guess that the problem would be as follows: I have been talking about putting men and women, young men and women, in positions of extreme danger and expecting them to, in a sense, to do something which is counterintuitive, which is to stay in a position of danger rather than get under cover or run from that position of danger. And if you have a military system which accepts that if it becomes dangerous you'll simply leave, then have you essentially systematic desertion. I just have a picture of an organisation that would fall apart very quickly. It simply could not be tolerated. Everything possible would be done to ensure it did not happen, and this is why in training you find a very pronounced emphasis on very low level loyalty between just one or two individual; the buddy system, it is called systems. You also emphasise loyalty to your unit and loyalty to your battalion and everything else and to your uniform, to your flag, you name it. It is all to do with your loyalty, all designed to try and keep you in position at a time when all your instincts are telling you that actually you should go, because, as I said, if you do decide together, and if the system somehow tolerates it, then it all looks to me as if it would fall apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you said the system would fall apart if persons were able to leave. To ask you a slightly different question, could any problems arise from individuals being spontaneously being able to join a military unit at will, without having to sign any agreement or undergo any official recruitment process?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Joining at well; just arriving?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, in a combat situation.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think it would generate a different set of problems, to be honest. If, let's say, you were a battalion commander or equivalent, with, I don't know, 5 or 600 men and women under command, and you wake up one morning and another hundred men have turned up and they say they want to fight for you, well, you have no idea and - I go back to Napoleon Bonaparte, you know, one bad general is better than two good ones - the battalion commander would not know where those people come from, how well were they trained, did they understand what was to be achieved, how long were they going to be stay, could they be trusted to remain. Actually, more to the point, if you don't know where they have come from and who they are, then there might be a security dimension to this: Am I going to trust them with all this information about my disposition on the battlefield and those of my accompanying units and so on. You simply wouldn't know who these people were, and I think there would be -- there would be some reluctance simply to accept these -- these -- well, not perhaps to accept them, but certainly to depend upon them in any really sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Is it important that an army be able to depend upon its members?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, and I won't labour the point about people being in stress and immense danger again. But I think what the system, the army, the hierarchy, has to do is to be able to depend on all subordinates in the structure, such that when an instruction is issued at the top of the system, with a view to it going all the way down to the bottom, that all those organisations in the system will be able and fit and inclined to do what is asked of them. If you can't have that dependability and trust, then the order is meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now a slightly different issue relating to the situation when a soldier joins an army. Is it normal for an army to keep records about such people joining a unit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you mean for an army to keep records of its -- its soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. There is a very advanced level of bureaucracy, certainly in the militaries that I have encountered, in a sense because you're dealing with -- there is a very complicated human resources operation going on. So there has to be a system of keeping records, of training, and health and promotion and discipline, and all that sort of thing. I guess, nowadays, it wouldn't be kept so much on paper and in personal files and it would be kept on computers, but there would be an effort to have a very close record of each person right the way down the system, so that you would know who they were, where they came from, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And could any problems arise for a superior commander if he did not have accurate information about the members of a subordinate unit beneath him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, there might be some, in a variety of ways. To return to our brigade commander, if he had a sense that one of his battalion commanders didn't know who was under his command, then there would be some question as to the effectiveness of that battalion commander, because the system, the battalion and the brigade and the division and so on, could not then have a good detailed sense of what that unit, that battalion is able to do, of what it is capable. It could be good or better or actually much worse than we think it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sure. Now, I want to move on to page 11 and it is the last sentence of paragraph 21, and this is connected to what you mentioned earlier in your testimony. And in this sentence, it says that: "The final point to note is that in modern armies the consent being granted by an individual is also to be subordinate do a political military system driven by an idea rather than to be subordinate to a specific leader." Can you explain for us a little further about this remark?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think -- yes, thank you. I think you could take a sort of a Hollywood view of military leadership, whereby the charismatic figure arrives on the battlefield and enthuses the troops, and off they go and they win a war. That has certainly happened in military history in medieval and ancient times. There is no doubt about that. It is still embodied, as I have been saying, in the idea of leadership and influence. It is still an important commodity. But, nowadays, this is a much more complicated system. And as I say here, generals will come ago go, they will be killed and injured, and so this complicated system has to be able to keep itself motivated and keep itself going. The way it has does that in, I would argue in Western liberal democracies, is ideally by being motivated by an idea rather than being motivated by the leader, whoever it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it is the time for the break. This might be an appropriate moment to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break until quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Cornish, before the break, we were talking about army units following a system rather than a particular leader. And in connection with that, I'd like to ask you this: Are there any traits by which an army unit would typically show that it is part of a system?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. If I may, Your Honour, before I answer that, could I make the point that, before the break, the transcript shows that I used the certainly "secondary mass grave," and I don't believe I did use that term. I can't remember exactly what I said, but I don't think I used that expression. Units would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. At what page and what line are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the screen now, it is at time 10.13.02.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. It is page 33, line 3 -- I apologise. It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Previous page, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Previous page line 8, 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Page 32, line 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What did you use? Dr. Cornish, do you remember what term you did use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm embarrassed to say that I can't exactly remember what term I did use, but I really don't think I used the term "secondary mass grave."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: With the assistance of the audio recording, it will be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, do you still recall the question, or would you like me to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I do. If I remember, the question was what traits or symbols or whatever a unit employ. Well, I think to mark its, to show its presence within the system, at the broadest level, the unit might be expected to wear the standard uniform. It might wear a badge of -- a cap badge. It might wear shoulder flashes, as they're known, to show that it is part of, not just that unit, but part of the bigger formation or structure to which it belongs. So there would be a shoulder flash to show that are you part of battalion A and part division 1, and so on. Then there will be, as well as an uniform and insignia, there would be flags and so on. And beneath all of that, there would also be - and, of course, you would not be able to see this, as this is nothing to see - but there would be common understanding and common doctrine. There would also be a sense in which they all work in, more or less, the same way and follow the same standards of training and deployment and operations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what if a unit did not display such typical traits, for example, it didn't wear army insignia or fly a flag, what conclusion could you draw, if any?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think one of two conclusions, either that this unit was a special unit; for example, a special forces units, a commando unit of some sort that was required not to wear any uniform or show any insignia in order that it could act covertly. That would be on possibility. Another interpretation, I think, would be that that unit considered itself apart from the organisation, and I think it would be at least unusual or would be perceived as unusual for this unit not to be behaving in the same corporate way that all the other units were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, so, if the unit did not act covertly but participated in regular combat, would that fall into the first category that you mentioned, special forces unit, or the second category?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think probably the second category, if they were -- and the military used the term "regular" to distinguish between, as it were, normal armed forces and those that are undertaking special operations. If a regular armed force were to be seen to be setting itself apart from the normal command structure, then it would be regarded as unusual, and perhaps even disloyal in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what would be the commander's responsibilities under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that a commander might well wish that sub-unit to -- because we are talking about, I think, a sub-unit attaching itself to a command structure, I think it would be, in those circumstances, reasonable for the senior commander to accept that that sub-unit was -- should behave as if it were a normal part of the command structure, wear the normal uniform, and so on. It should adopt the same demonstrations of loyalty and team-working as all other units; otherwise, there would have to be some explanation why it didn't do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what happens if it doesn't, if it doesn't fall in line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then, this either becomes a matter of discipline, the subordinate commander might have been given an instruction to wear the standard uniform, or whatever; and then there's a matter, as I said, of military discipline between the senior and subordinate commander. Assuming all the time that this sub-unit is presenting itself as part of the hierarchy, then I think it would have to be dealt with as a disciplinary matter. Otherwise, I think the senior commander would be excused for thinking and for supposing that this subunit, in spite of what was being said, was actually running according to its own means or its own aspirations in some way. The point I'm getting at is that he would not feel that if this subunit could pass that very basic test of wearing the same uniform and supporting the same insignia and so on, then perhaps he might not be able to trust it in time of conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier about the Hollywood-style of leadership and how armies try to move away from that, so that units do not follow a specific leader. What I'd like to ask you is: What if a unit only recognised the authority of certain individuals within an army and attempted to obtain directions directly from such persons outside of the regular chain of command, what conclusions, if any, could you draw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then, I would say that a traditional analysis of these things would suggest that this unit was not part of the command chain of the hierarchy and did not respect the notion of unity of command, and I would draw and all of the points that I've made earlier this morning, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to move to, it's page 11, paragraph 23 -- sorry. Before we turn to that, paragraph 22, where the heading is "Purpose." In this paragraph, you talk about command being concerned by with the purposeful of military means to achieve a military, strategic, and, ultimately, political end. Could you elaborate on this a little, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I think behind this paragraph is something of my own interpretation and my own understanding; and, therefore, my -- I suppose my political, philosophical preferences, in that I believe in Western liberal democracies. Liberal force should be used only to achieve a political purpose. When that purpose is achieved, the civil political control should reassert itself entirely. As I say here, I think, if a military organisation pursues something other than a political purpose, and if it is -- or if its goal is the use of military force as an end in itself, then that, as far as I can see and as far as I would interpret and explain things, that would be closer to militarism.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And are you alone when you take this point of view or are there others sharing this opinion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think I would be supported in that point by every person who has read and understood and agrees with the writings of Carl von Clausewitz, who, as an early nineteenth century Prussian strategist and who, many would argue, in the word which I come from, in the teaching of strategic studies and so on, is the person who more than any other has understood in the modern era the relationship between the use of armed force and the civil political control of that -- of that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In the next paragraph of your report, paragraph 23, you state that the relationship between the military activity and political goal is one which is widely taught and understood in modern armed forces, and then you go on to use the term "levels of war." What is the origins of the term "levels of war"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This is another -- another difficult question. I think a similar question was asked earlier. Again, it is really part of the fundamental understanding of the way a military is organised between strategic and operational and tactical. I think you can certainly find this expression on the worldwide web, if you were to Google it, and I believe you could even find it on Wikipedia. But you don't find, I don't think, a definitive source for this term because it is so widespread and so widely understood. That said, there is another late 18th, early 19th century French military strategist, Baron Antoine Henri de Gomani - just Gomani would work - who referred to a political and a tactical and a strategic level. So he is often attributed as the source of this idea in the modern era for a division between levels. But I think it goes back much further and is part of military common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And you say that this relationship between military activity and political goal is widely taught. Where would these concepts be taught?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Really, from the moment that you begin military training, and I'd argue probably at any level. So this isn't just something that would be confined to officers and leaders. It would be taught broadly across the military system. So it would be in basic training organisations; in military academies, such as the one I attended, the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst; and it would be taught in staff colleges, such as the one that I taught at, the Joint Services Command and Staff College in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at the levels of war in a little more detail, can you explain for us what is the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: As I say in the paper, this is the level at which national security policy and defence strategy are decided. It used to be -- some people used to think in terms of their being two strategic levels: A political level and a military level, political strategy and military strategy. I prefer, and I think I would say a lot of people, now prefer just the one term. At this highest level, there is within government a capacity to decide when and how and for what reason to use armed force. That decision making process is not entirely civil and political; it is informed by military expertise. So, at that highest strategic level, you have civil decision informed by military expertise, and the output should be a strategic decision or instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Moving to the operational level, are you able to elaborate for us what that is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: There can be some confusion in the word -- in the use of the term "operations." All military use the term "operations" as an euphemism for combat, as in: I have been on operations or we are on operations in Iraq and Afghanistan and so on. The operational level is doctrinally something different. It is at the level of divisions and brigades, where the commanders are using their military force to implement or to give effect to the strategic decision. So, at that level, they are commanders, soldiers and commanders of military forces. That is all they do. They are not in the business of political debate. They are professional military people undertaking military tasks, but they do so in order to give effect to the strategic division which has come down to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then, finally, could you elaborate upon the tactical level of war, please.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, this is fighting. This is contact, as it is termed in the military, with an enemy, in order to achieve the operational goal which has been passed down to you. So it is actually, if you like, the operational is planning the use of your force and manoeuvring them into place, and then the tactics is actually undertaking the fighting or the capturing or whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, returning to the strategic level, what sorts of tasks and duties would the professional head of an army - and by that, I mean the most senior military officer in an army - working at the strategic level typically carry out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: At that level, in government, the professional military head; that is to say, let me use the UK as an example, each armed service in the UK has a professional military head. There's a chief of the General Staff for the army; there's a chief of the air staff for the air force; and there's a first sea lord for the navy, a curious historical blip there. Each of those is the professional head of their armed service, and their duty, in a sense, is to represent their armed service in this political military decision making process. It happens that, in the UK, their reputation of their service is funneled or channel by one further level, which is a chief of the Defence staff who is their chief, and that person ought to ensure that all of this professional expertise and advice goes through to the political process. The assumption, I think, behind this is that this is such a difficult and arcane activity that it would be unreasonable to expect political leaders to know absolutely what could and could not be achieved. So when they are at the point of making -- or deliberating and making these decisions, they would need to have people in this system at this very high level who could say, actually, you can't use, I don't know, one division to do more than one thing or whatever. So it would be an advisory capacity at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just dealing with the professional head of the army, how would that person typically direct his subordinates? What would he do?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: So this would be the professional head of an army in, let's say, a capital representing his armed service?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: At this level, it really isn't so much of a matter of command in the way I have been describing it early, for units and formation atlas are going to be deployed on combat. At this very high level, it really is more like the management of a business. So you would have a chief executive officer, and, of course, he is in charge, but around him are specialists. There would be a chief financial officer; there would be someone in charge of human resources; there would be someone in charge of equipment; someone in charge of recruitment; so on and so forth. And all those people, although subordinate to the chief, in a sense, they are experts in their own right. So it is not is much a matter of ordering. The chief, there is no order that he could give to, I don't know, a director of equipment, other than, for example, "We need to make sure that we can equip our armed forces correctly." That is generally understood anyway. That is what he is there for, in the first place. So it is a slightly different atmosphere at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now I'd like to turn to the part of your report that deals with military control, and we can find this at page 14 and onwards. In the preamble at the top of the page, we can see, in the last sentence, you say that military control involves the following: Command infrastructure, planning, communications and liaison, information, intelligence and reporting, logistics and supply, and discipline. What is the basis for your making that statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, very close to the basis for responding to an earlier comment, in that I have been working in analysing, teaching, and explaining this often curious world for some 25 years. And if asked how I do think a military control system works, those are the elements I would say are essential to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to the first element, which is command infrastructure, and you use an example of a typical operational headquarters at the level of a brigade or a division, and you said that is the specialist within that headquarters. Again, it may be a simple question: Why is the command headquarters divided into different specialist areas?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Do you mean what I have shown here, the G1, G2, G3, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is the example-- no, no. I'm talking about them more broadly, I believe. Perhaps you could just explain why a command is divided up into different specialist areas?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Really, because at this level -- well, perhaps I could go back to one step. At a lower level, all of these have to be dealt with. At any level of command, someone has to be making sure that -- that the food is there and the fuel is there. So all these things have to be happening. But at very low level, because ipso facto, this is a small organisation, it is possible for one person to undertake more than one task. So you could have at a battalion level, and I speak from experience, it could be possible for an officer to be in charge of operational planning and to be in charge of human resource planning. It's thought that that is a reasonable way of doing things, and it is feasible. As you get higher up the chain of command and as the organisation fattens, the task is simply bigger, so you need a specialist in each of these areas. And as you get to the top of the command chain where the task is enormous, you find within each other area another small command chain has built up. So there would be a specialist in, I don't know, in ammunition supply; then beneath him, he might have sub-specialists, one whom works on rifle ammunition, let's say, and another one who works on artillery ammunition. So you just make sure that everything is covered at the level at which it is needed and with the capacity that it is needed, is the point I make, I think, with the capacity that is needed at the right level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So at the highest level, within a specialist department, you would find sub-specialisation; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, you could, absolutely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, moving away from that on page 15, paragraph 30, you state that -- and this is the penultimate sentence at the paragraph at the top of the page. You say that any commander must, of course -- must also, of course, presuppose obedience and dependability on the part of his subordinate commanders, and a subordinate unit will be expected to be able and prepared to carry out instructions. I believe you have touched upon this earlier, but can you explain what you mean by that sentence?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I mean this: That when a senior -- when any commander, when any commander is given a task or a mission, he then looks to his or her resources and begins planning to go meet that mission. And as he does so, unless there is some special reason to suppose otherwise, if, for example, one of his sub- units, to use an earlier example, is exhausted or is full of new recruits or whatever, then he would adjust his plan accordingly. But without that special reasoning, he would, or she, would assume that the units and facilities and resources under his command would available. They would be absolutely critical to the planning presumptions and suppositions he would begin to make. He couldn't go into planning with, I don't know, moving one battalion to the left and one to the right, if he didn't know that those battalions would do as he said they would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in the scenario that have you just mentioned where a commander is ordering a battalion from the left to the right, or, in fact, issuing any type of instruction, would the commander normally expect to receive confirm from the subordinate unit that the order or instruction has been carried out?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I think he would, usually, in fact, if not always. As I just said, the senior commander would assume that the subordinate commander and unit would do as instructed, and the senior commander would then need to know, because is he in command and running everything, he would need to know that his instruction has been carried out. So, typically, let's say, you would find the subordinate commander informing his superior that he had carried out the task as instructed.
