Importantly, if he had been unable to carry out the task as instructed, because of some difficulty, because he ran out of fuel or met the enemy or something, then it would be crucial to pass that information to the superior, so that the superior is then in a position to adjust the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to reporting in more detail in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This relates to what I asked you a little earlier before we took the break. I hear you saying here that, to use an earlier example, if a battalion is exhausted or is full of new recruits or whatever, then he would adjust his plan accordingly. Earlier, when I asked you this question, you said that he could talk back to the senior, and are you able to reconcile these two apparent inconsistencies? I'm not suggesting that there are inconsistencies, but I am just saying that I am understanding you slightly differently now. Now it seem as if the subordinate commander is expected to adjust his plan. Earlier, I got the impression that he could talk back and say, "I'm sorry, Mr. Senior Commander, I can't that job, because my troops are tired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise for any confusion or any inconsistency I might have suggested. I don't think there is inconsistency. What I am trying describe is a system which is iterative at every level. So a commander in the middle of this system would be given a task by his superior, he would then interrogate his subordinates to be sure that he knows exactly what the level of the fitness of the units are and if there are any problems so on and so forth. On the assumption that if there are no special problems, then a unit must be there and be dependable and able to do what is asked for it. He would then be able to report to his superior that the order that has been given has bee met. So I'm not suggesting that there is debate. I'm not suggesting that there is refusal or anything to accept an instruction, but there is discussion about how best to achieve it. That goes on through the system, and there are a series of exchanges of information. So the superior asks the subordinates, and the subordinates ask their subordinates, and so on. Then it repeats back up the chain of command, such that in the end the mission or the task can be completed. So there is a constant flow of instructions and requests an information going back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess the point where I asked the question and where I still need a bit of clarity is in the event that a subordinate unit or the commander of a subordinate unit, say, is unable to carry out the task. As you given the examples that you gave, he has got new troops or he is troops are tired, can he say or can he send word back and say, "Sorry, Mr. Senior, I'm not able to carry out this task because my troops are tired."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would happen, Your Honour, more like this: In the process of briefing and giving orders, that commander would say this is difficult for me for the following reasons, and explains his position to the superior. His superior is then in a position of knowing what the compatibilities are of his resources; and then it is for him to make the decision. Of course, he might, even so, still decide to send that unit to do the task, but at least he does so from the basis of knowledge. That what is what is so critical, that he must know what his subordinate units and commanders are capable of all the time, and he can only know that on the basis of the information or regular information flows or, indeed, at that planning meeting that would take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just to pick up on that last answer, you said that the superior commander could still decide to send the unit to do the task. If the superior commander issued an order to a subordinate unit to complete a task, knowing that, for example, its men may be tired, could the subordinate commander of the unit point blank refuse to carry out the order?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: No. I do apologise if I have given this impression, that it is open to refuse. It is imperative to give advice and information on the state of your unit to your superior, so that the superior knows ideally what he can and cannot expect of you. But in some circumstances, it might well be that your under-resourced unit is the best one that he has, your superior; and, therefore, he might decide that that is the one, nevertheless, that will be used; because in the end, the superior is running to an order that he has been given, that he has to meet, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: We'll come to reporting in a little more detail in a moment. Before that, I would like to touch on the part of your report that deals with planning, and this is it at page -- it's page 15 and it is here in front of us. You talk about the different types of planning, at the different levels. In terms of planning at the strategic level, you say that this involves careful articulation of long-range objectives. In what ways would you normally expect these strategic objectives to be expressed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: The use of the term "long-range objectives" here is, in part, to distinguish the strategic level from the operational and tactical, which are much more immediate. What I mean by long-range objectives, at this strategic level, well, really, we might be talking about defend the country or defeat the enemy. These are the biggest possible ideas you can imagine. We have decided to use armed force in order to rescue this, defeat that, or whatever, a big long-term goal that has to be pursued. So, in strict military terms, it doesn't have much meaning, but it is the context in which everything below is to take place and is to happen. As you go further down the chain, right down at the bottom, the objective becomes take that hill or capture that building. But it is done in the context of the high level strategic goal which is to whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. And, in this paragraph, you say that a commander issuing a plan should set out orders to be achieved and why, but the how should be left to subordinates. Can you explain for us why this is and what would the consequences of a commander telling his subordinates how to carry out a plan?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. This expresses an idea which is very common; in fact, it is fundamental in certainly Western European and US and many other countries in the world that have trained in, if I can call it, the sort of Western European way. There is probably a better expression for that, but I don't have it. The idea is that you have very well trained and very capable young people who are in a position of junior leadership, as well as being soldiers or whatever, as well as being military professionals, and the thinking is that you should have a system which allows them to use their imagination and their knowledge and their initiative, more to the point, to respond as accurately as anyone can to the immediate situation. This is critical. What is required is that there should be somebody, somewhere who can produce the most suitable response to the problem at hand, and the thinking is the way to achieve that is by trusting in the subordinate that is confronting that problem, rather than issuing from on high, from, you know, miles on high, a direct order as to how such-and-such a thing should be achieved. In strategic thinking, there are very broadly two approaches, and they both employ German terms. One is [German spoken] which is order based tactics. You only do what are you instructed to do and nothing else. The modern, much more dynamic approach is known as [German spoken] which is extraction. You understand what your superior is to do, and you, then, as a junior, undertake your mission in order to achieve that. But are you trusted at that level to do your job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is part of the answer to that also not that the junior official is closer to the situation and understands better than the senior commander who is a little far removed and he would know the how. You know, if I say take that hill, in order to approach it from the south or the east, or from the east or the west, or from or both sides, you know, that's his little plan, his attack plan. You couldn't prescribed that from him from a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You shouldn't. That is precisely the argument. You do occasionally find some commanders, in all armies or forces, who believe it is their task to give micro-detailed instructions: Attack the hill from the north only. That is just perceived as militarily nonsense, because that person clearly has a view and the responsibility of something, but it is very wide and very broad and complex. What he doesn't have, as you said, sir, is that view of the hill and the best to get to the top of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In terms of planning at the different level us that mention, strategic, operational, and tactical, does the type of information and level of detail needed to plan vary at those different levels?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It certainly does, yes. At a very low level, if you were a low-level commander in charge of 30 soldiers, what is known as a platoon, then you would expect to have at your fingerer tips information as to, for example, the number of rifle cartridges each soldier had, down to, you know, the difference between 20 and 30 would be important; how many water bottles each of them had; really micro-information. But what that platoon commander would then pass up to his company commander would be a consolidated version of that; either that "We, my platoon, we need another 100 rounds of ammunition or we need another three cannisters of water." As it goes further up the chain of command, so the information is more and more consolidated, it would be ludicrous, for example, for a divisional commander to be beleaguered with information as to how many water bottles each soldier in his 8.000-manned division was carrying. He doesn't need or want to have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I want to deal with paragraph 32, which is communications at the bottom of the page. And in this paragraph, you explain how each level communicates with the level above and also the level below, and you give the example of a platoon commander communicates with his section commander below, but also he communications with his company commander above. This goes up and down throughout the chain of command. What happens if a commander at a certainly level, for example, let's say the brigade level, does not report to his immediate superior at the divisional level but jumps that level and reports to the corps commander two levels above him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: There might be special circumstances in which that would take place. The brigade commander might be, as it were, detached from the normal chain of command and undertaking a specific task for the corps commander. This is also commonplace. But what is key is that everybody would know that this was taking place. It would be a very special arrangement. So the division, which would be nominally responsible for the brigade in question, would understand that the brigade had been detached and was now answering to the corps, and, therefore, would not expect or require reports from the brigade and would understand what was happening. So there wouldn't be any conflict. If, though, a brigade under normal circumstances were to decide for itself to report outside or around the chain of command to a senior level, a more senior level, then that would be, as I said earlier, to contradict the principle of unity of command and would be to go outside the chain of command, which is an anathema, and that whole structure begins to become inoperable. People don't know who is doing what, with what resources, for what means, for what ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: A linked question, and perhaps similar to something we touched upon earlier. What if a commander of a military unit, instead of reporting to his immediate superior in the chain of command, sought to report directly to and receive instructions from the highest political levels of the state to which the army belonged?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, that would be to step outside of the command chain with rather massive self-confidence, I would have to say. It would be such a flagrant abuse of the whole system, and it would also send, I think, a very peculiar message, that this unit considers itself to be in some kind of special relationship with the political leadership. Now, as I think I have been saying, there might be circumstances in which a very small unit could almost answer directly to a political leader. It is very common practice to use very, very small units of special forces, down to a handful of men, half a dozen, four; and they could exactly send reports straight back to the head of government. But as I keep saying, that would be a special arrangement that everybody would understand: That is the way that part of the military system works. For a regular, normal unit to do the same thing would be presumptuous, to say the lest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your report you stress the importance of a commander having a clear, accurate, and realtime picture of everything taking place within his area of responsibility through the receipt of report. Can I ask you what if a subordinate unit is comprised of soldiers that do not speak the same language as a superior commander? How important is it that there is a common basis for communication?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It is very important, of course, and the ideal would be that all units and all troops would speak the same language. But military organisations have long since got round this problem, because it is conceivable that you could be certainly in an alliance, so you could be fighting alongside troops from other country. The way to get round it is by use of a specialist known as a liaison officer, and LO. Liaison officers would be deployed where ever necessary to act as a bridge between the different units from different countries and with different language. Obviously, that person would have to be proficient in the languages relevant. That is one way round it. The other way round it, and I speak I think largely from experience and knowledge of the way the North Atlantic Treaty has done this, you standardise as far as you possibly can the way those different nationalities do things. You have standard agreements on how forces are moved, how they will replenish themselves, and so on. So you try to standardise everything. So even though there are language difficulties the organisation, as a whole, works as coherently as it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what sort of problems could arise if those features are not in place; In other words, there is no liaison officer or standard agreement, if you're able to say?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, I would imagine there would be little possibility of the commanders, either side of this unit in question, understanding what that unit was going on -- was doing; and that, therefore, brings us back to this problem in military thinking of operational security. It would not be possible to know that that unit had received and understood its orders in the same way that all the other units had received and understood their orders because of a linguistic difficulty, and it would not be possible to know exactly what they were doing because nobody can understand what they are saying. Translation would be crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in -- in the combat situation where there's ongoing fighting, how important is speed in terms of passing information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Very, very important. But there has to be a balance struck between speed and accuracy. If could I give one illustration of this: At a very low level, if a unit comes into contact with an enemy force and is fired upon, the requirement is that it should pass as much information as it possibly can to the next level up, and so on, up the command chain, so that the end a corps commander would understand that part of his formation has made contact with the enemy. But the first requirement for that soldier who has made contact with the enemy is not to get out books and pamphlets and start writing lengthy reports and sending them by radio or whatever, it is actually to do what a soldier must do, which is respond to the contact and start shooting back or whatever else is required. So you would have two things happen: You would have an immediate report which is sent, which simply can be one word, "contact," which goes all the way up the command chain. Everybody understands what that means, "We are now in touch with the enemy." It would be followed by, "Wait out," or equivalence in military communications. That means, "I'm in contact. I'm a little bit busy at the moment. But as soon as I have dealt with the problem, I can tell you exactly what has happened." It would be followed up by a detailed contact report: It was, in the end, only three men, or actually it looks a bit bigger than that, and this could be quite important. That information would then go back. So there has got to be a balance between alerting and informing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And what the consequences if that sort of information is not passed up to the superior commander?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then the superior commander could not know, unless he had some other means of knowing, and I can't think what they meet be, unless he had some sort of satellite or aerial surveillance or something, that commander could not know that arguably the most important aspect of military activity had begun. And if the commander doesn't know that, then this is disastrous: What is he to do, how is he to move his force around, what does it actually mean, is this a big part of the enemy or a small part. I am talking, obviously, in very basic terms here, but I hope I am explaining my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Sure. Now, at paragraph 36, you deal with information, intelligence, and reporting; and paragraph 36 deals with what you have just mentioned, the requirement to report enemy activity. If we turn over to the page, on to page 17, you also talk about the need to report other information, such as food and water. So apart from reporting enemy activity and reporting on food and water status, are there any other issues that a unit should provide information on, on a regular basis, to its superior?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: If it -- as much information as really is necessary. I mean, this is fairly open-ended. The obvious ones, as you said, would be those resources which are essential to the immediate task: Ammunition, food, and water, and so on. There would also, though, if it were a mechanised unit, it would want to let the command chain know its fuel status. That would usually be expressed in terms of -- not in terms of how many gallons I have or how many litres of diesel fuel I have, but how many days of movement time I have able to me. All that information would have to be passed back, and you could also pass back casualty information. I have 30 men and they're all fit and uninjured. I have 30 men, but two of them have been slightly injured, three of them have got some sort of food or water-borne illness but they are still able to fight, and so on. So you just pass as much information as you can relevant to your circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, typically, how often should this information be passed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It would be passed routinely on a daily basis from low level all the way back up. So there would be this really constant awareness. The military use a term "situational awareness," and that has two parts. It is knowing as closely as you possibly can what your adversary is doing, but it is also knowing as closely as you possibly can what your own forces are capable of and where they are and what they might be confronting. So there is -- in many ways, it is surprising. There is an enormous requirement for the flow of information, constantly. In a sense, if a unit doesn't supply the information constantly on a daily basis, that becomes an indicator of some sort of a problem. So it can actually have other uses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me that my last question and your answer overlaps, and I apologise because I might perhaps be speaking a little quickly. If I just bear with me a moment. I don't know if it is something that be corrected at a later stage. We can see that there is a cue placed at next to what, I believe, was the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robson, you never take account of the fact that the what is being said is also translated in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we don't make presumptions, Mr. Robson --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- why don't you ask the witness to repeat the answer to the question where the cue is, so that we know what answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Dr. Cornish. I will ask that you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Typically, how often should this information be passed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: My response to that question begins with the words, "It would be passed routinely on a daily basis from low level all the way back up," and then the remainder of the answer follows.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I can hear the interpretation on General Delic's headphones as well, so I will bear that in mind, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I can hear the interpretation behind me, so I will use that as an indicator as to when to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you wanted him to reduce the volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as to information about the situation in a unit such as combat results and personnel states, what if a unit did not send a report to its superior command, but instead sent that information to an entity or body outside of the army organisation, what conclusions, if any, could you draw?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This then takes this is issue to the next level of presumptuousness. Bad enough to skip one level in the command chain; much worse to skip it altogether and go to the political leadership; and then completely inconceivable that it could go to a different political leadership. What on earth is going on? I wouldn't really know how to describe that situation, in the absence of there being a multi-national alliance operation of some sort, whereby you could have a certain national unit reporting through its national command chain, alongside another national command chain. But the idea that a body that was nominally integrate the within one command chain, could report to a completely different politico-military system, I would be baffled. I wouldn't really know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 37 deals with logistics and supply. Where would a military unit typically get its weapons, ammunition, equipment, and food from?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: The weapons you would normally -- they would be issued and they would be part of the combat organisation of that unit; and so, you know, you would have whatever you, as an infantry battalion, required to be a infantry battalion. It would be given to you. Then as far as the re-supply is concerned, each unit, even a very low level, a very small unit, would have a certain amount of re-supply capacity. You could imagine, even at a very low level, of a section of troops of eight infantrymen, that there might be someone carrying spare ammunition or there might be a place where they had a bit of spare water or whatever. So there would be very low level re-supply. Otherwise, whole system depends upon a very elaborate and very complicated, complex, and extensive logistics operation which begins as far back as you can imagine with enormous amounts of container traffic, and everything on air traffic and so on, that then just delivers and pushes all this materiel further and further forward, until the point at which it is used. I think I gave some figures there from the first Gulf War, just to give some idea of how much can be involved. Obviously, this was a very large military operation, but I think it is indicative of what the material referred to as a logistic tail, the size of the operation that must exist behind the actual military head of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And would it be unusual or -- let me ask that a different way. What conclusions could you draw, if any, if a material unit was outside the regular supply chain, in that it received money, weapons, ammunition, equipment, and food from sources external to the army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: At some level, there has always been and will always be within armed forces the ability, in fact the necessity, to requisition. So let me give you another simple example. If you are a commander of a unit which moves around on trucks, and your trucks run out of fuel, then it might make sense, militarily, rather than wait for the logistics system to produce fuel tankers that can come forward to your position and refuel you, it might make sense, if you come across such a thing, to refuel those vehicles, through a requisition, from a civil fuel station which you happen to come across. Likewise, food; throughout military history, armies have always used local resources to nourish themselves, sometimes often in a more civilised way than at others. Sometimes it is more of a contract that is struck and payments are made or promissory notes are given at other times. As we know from military history, it is simply a matter of just taking everything that you can and, as is described, living off the land. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So forgive me for a long-winded first part of an answer. But when it comes to other things like weapons and ammunition and equipment, then you're getting into the real, in a sense, the life blood of this system, because if the system doesn't have a close understanding of the expenditure rates of ammunitions and fuel, and so on, of all of its units, and the only way to get that understanding is through reports and requisitions or requirements -- I'm sorry, requirements for more ammunition and so on, if it doesn't have that understanding, then it can't form a picture of how capable that unit is. It might that be the unit has got ammunition from somewhere else because it came across some or it is refueled from somewhere else; but if it doesn't know that that has happened through the normal system, then there can't be much confidence that that unit will be able to do what is expected of it. As for money, this is not something that I have never come across. No, I wouldn't know how that could work, not in the least. It does, apart from very low level, it does tend, in times of operations and conflict, it tends to run something like a cashless economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would say about, if anything with respect to this point, the use of booty for replenishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean the use of captured treasures of some sort or money?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exactly. It could have been money, it could have been fuel, it could have been food, it could have been ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I guess I won't be naive enough to suggest that won't ever happen. Of course, it does happen and will continue to happen. But I would say that, in an established military system of the sort with which I'm familiar, that should not happen, for a number of reasons: Partly because it is not thought to be the best way to treat those people in whose territory you are operating; but also more seriously, militarily, there has to be quality control as to what is provided. So there has to be confidence that when a unit is given fuel, that that is the right fuel, it is high quality fuel and is able to fuel their engines, and that the ammunition is of a certain quality, and that it will at least fit the guns that they are going to be firing with. So there has to be quality control, which could be completely absent. What you describe, of course, happens, but I think for established armies and armed forces, this is not considered a professional way of doing things, and it also has professional penalties in terms of the passage of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question on this particular aspect. To supply or re-supply, you spoke about the possibility to requisition, commandeer. Would it also be acceptable to have voluntary contributions, instead of pretending, by requisitioning or commandeering, to re-supply by payment? Would it be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess it could. I don't know of a circumstances in which it has taken place, but I can certainly imagine that it might do. However, I would say that if there were to be an organisation or an individual or some sponsor somewhere willing to do such a thing, then it would be preferable for that offer to be made at the high level to support the overall operation, because what you would try to avoid are these idiosyncrasies, these little curiosities of who has what and where did they get it from. Indeed, there might be a loyalty that I mentioned to this. If this unit is supported specifically by its own logistics, re- supply route, what does that mean entirely? What is actually going on? Can we really depend on them once again, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, if there was a military unit that did not depend upon the regular supply chain for its resources and had independent financial support, could such a situation have an impact on the command and control over that unit, are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. That's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll do is I'll reformulate the question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if you're able to say, and if you can't help me, please say so, what consequences might stem from a unit receiving external resources and financial support?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would, again, say that it invites questions as to the level of integration of that unit within the overall system and, indeed, of the dependability of that unit, for all the reasons I've given. Really, there would not be a clear idea, there could not be a clear idea of precisely what that unit was capable of, if it were not reporting and requiring through the standard logistics chain of its needs. Yes, I think I'd leave it that the. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just a couple of small issues to deal with, and I'm looking at the clock, so I think it would be an appropriate time to take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is, indeed. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, I'd now like to take you to the part of your report which deals with discipline, and specifically what I'm interested in is at page 19 of the report at paragraph 44. And in talking about military discipline, in this paragraph, we can see that you say the exercise of military discipline also makes three other presumptions. The first is obvious to the point of being banal, in that it is presupposed that the individuals upon who military discipline is to be exercised are highly trained soldiers. Now, are you able to just elaborate on that comment forever us, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm referring to here is the idea that we have touched on already, that there is something of a contract between the soldier and commander, soldier and system, if you like; that it is a specific sort of contract that enables and requires these specific sort of disciplinary measures. That is really all I'm really getting at. That it is such a unique framework of human interaction that you would not expect or require to use that framework in other circumstances, such as running your family or being a head of your family or running a business. So it requires and presupposes that the people involved in this system have all undergone this training and have entered into, by whatever means, this contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Then the final presumption you refer to, towards the bottom of the paragraph, you say: "Again almost in a banal way, the exercise of military discipline also presupposes a degree of physical security from enemy attack." Could you please elaborate on that remark?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. All I mean by this is that beyond the most immediate level where, in a way, you're really talking about an expectation off being disciplined, rather than having to discipline, beyond that level, in a military legal system, in the UK system it would be broadly analogous to going through the magistrate level, then to crown court and appeal court, and so on. It is, obviously, complicated and complex, and it is not -- in the normal course of events, it would not be possible to run that sort of structure, either when your army is moving somewhere or deploying or certainly when you are being attacked, because then you have, as I said - I hope we're not being flippant - then you have other things, more pressing things, on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. And if we can move now to the final topic of my questions, and this is it at page 22 in the section that deals with military failure; paragraph 52, failure ever military control. You repeat the point you made earlier that effective military control has at least six key functional areas, and you mention the six areas or features that we've discussed today. Then you conclude: "The absence or inadequacy of any one of these six key functions would lead to failure of military control." Please, can you tell me, what is the basis of you making that statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: This really follows my earlier response, that this analysis that I've given is based on, you know, my life and my career and my scholarship and experience of these things. I've thought very hard. When I was writing, I need to say, I thought very hard how would I describe a typical military control system. It would involve these elements, and I'm confident in saying that this would be understood, generally, in military circles. Then the next question is: Well, what happens? Are any of these disposal? I really can't see -- in looking at the list now, I really can't see how this complicated management system could work without any one of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Dr. Cornish. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move to admit the report and Dr. Cornish's CV into evidence. So the report is D1034 and the CV is D1035.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The report, D1034, and the CV, D1035 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number, a joint exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, both exhibits will become 1383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Cornish.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and, along with my colleagues here, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I would, sir, ask you to follow, basically, the same guidelines that my learned friend Mr. Robson did. We speak a similar language, I wouldn't go as far as to say the same language, a similar language. We need to pause between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters and the court reporter. Let me go back, sir, to just a few of the items that you testified about earlier today, and I'm going to start with something that was discussed on pages 36 and 37 of the transcript. I'll go back to refresh your memory as to exactly it was that you testified about. You were asked some questions by the Presiding Judge in the context of members of a unit that perhaps weren't wearing standard uniforms and the relationship in that situation to military discipline. Do you remember that subject, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Part of what you said - and this is reflected on page 36, lines 2 through 9 - you said: "Otherwise, I think the senior commander would be excused for thinking and for supposing that this sub- unit, in spite of what was being said, was actually running according to its own means or its own aspirations in some way, and the point I'm getting at is that he would not feel that if this sub-unit could pass that very basic test of wearing the same uniform and supporting the same insignia and so on, then perhaps he might not be able to trust it in the time of conflict." Do you remember that part of your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, in this type of situation where this sub-unit might not wear standard uniforms, would your answer be any different, sir, if that unit were, nevertheless, being given assignments and carrying out those assignments, notwithstanding the fact that they weren't wearing standard uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then, yes, I think it would. But I would imagine, then, that we would be talking about some sort of alliance structure, rather than a single unitary national structure or unitary command structure. If I remember correctly, the discussion that you have just summarized also involved at the point that an order would have been given to this unit, to change its uniform or wear a different insignia or whatever, and I think the question was: What would you infer from its failure or refusal to do so? I think that was my response. As I said, it is, of course, perfectly conceivable that there can be alliance operations, but it would be known about. I was given to understand that this would be -- that the scenario that we were discussing was a different unit, a different sort of unit from some unknown origin that, in a sense, refused to integrate itself with the home command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is a fair enough comment, sir. Let me just take that same scenario, again based upon your expertise in these matters, the situation where the unit is ordered to bring itself into compliance with respect to uniforms, insignia, et cetera, the unit doesn't do that; nevertheless, the unit is given combat taskings and assignments and carries those out, notwithstanding the fact that with respect to the more mundane issue of their uniforms and their non-compliance with an order to bring themselves in line in that respect, they nevertheless are given combat assignment and carried them out. What would your opinion in that situation be?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then I think my opinion would be: So far, so good. If the commander has given instructions to this units and it's all worked well, then fine; but my point remains, and it is the point that I have been trying to make. I would argue that there could not be that same level of reliability, communications, dependability, and so on, that the commander could except from other units. There would be certain indications, certain signals that this unit is refusing to fully integrated and wear the uniform or whatever, and those signals presumably mean something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your opinion there, on this point, remains the same even though, in terms of more important issues, such as combat assignments and carrying those outside, that unit still complied?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think, as I said earlier, in a sense, the most important aspect of military activity is fighting. That's what they're all there for. So if this unit is able to do what -- the job it is given and can contribute, then fine. But almost the second important aspect is this whole process of planning and expectation that in the future, after this given operation, they could then do another one, or whatever. It could work well, but it still seems to me to be something slightly apart from the standard arrangement that I have been describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if those orders to engage in combat operations continued, again notwithstanding the fact that members of the unit failed to comply with uniform regulations, what would -- what would be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then, again, it seems to be working and it is working fine, but for how much longer? Is there going to become a point at which the commander of this attached unit will decide on his own terms or on somebody else's terms or whatever, either superior have no idea, that that commander might decide that it has gone on long enough and, therefore, is withdraw ing his contribution. When it works, it works well, as you describe; but it might not work forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me, then, go to another question and answer that you gave earlier this morning. This is it reflected on page 31 of the transcript, and my learned colleague Mr. Robson was talking to you about the need for record keeping in the context of personnel matters. Do you remember that subject, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The question he put to you, reflected on lines 8 through 10 of page 31, is the following: "Could any problems arise from a superior commander if he did not have accurate information about the members of a subordinate unit beneath him?" Let me ask you this, Dr. Cornish: What level or degree of information would the superior need to know about members of a subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It's really more to the point that the superior officer would expect his subordinate officer to have that knowledge and to be reporting whatever parts of it need to be reported, because that level of knowledge or that understanding of your troops is an essential intrinsic part of military command. So if that subordinate officer is unable to provide information or doesn't want to, or whatever, then that would be an indication that actually that commanding officer is not perhaps fully in command or not in command in the ways that might be expected of them; and, therefore, it then feeds back into this whole issue about the confidence with -- in which the superior can give orders and instructions to his subordinate. It would be an indicator that there would be possibly something wrong. Just to finish the point, there would always be certain types of detailed personnel information that would have to be going back up the chain of command all the time, specifically, and most obviously, to do with injuries. And if that cannot happen for some reason, then that, likewise, is as bad as not able to pass on information about ammunition and fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Right. Let me just ask a few follow-on questions, then. Would it be an impairment on the ability of a corps commander to lead a corps if he didn't know the identity of soldiers in a company or a battalion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: No. It would, though, if I may continue, be an impairment on his ability as a corps commander if his division, brigade, battalion, and company commanders did not know the identity. That is the point I'm make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, we're going, actually, sir, work our way right down the chain of command to that very point. We wouldn't expect the division commander to know the identity of the soldiers at the company level, now, would we?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I don't think it would be necessary. I think I made a point earlier that you wouldn't know a divisional commander to know how many water bottles each soldier was carrying. It is not necessary, but it is necessary that someone in the system does have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly. We could do the same exercise going down. The brigades commander is not going to know the identity of the soldiers in the companies; the battalion commander very well might not know the identity of all the individuals in the companies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think so. There becomes a point at which it becomes more humanly possible for an individual to know a certain number of people, and there have been studies on this. I think you might expect, at a battalion level of about, let's say, between 500 and 700 men and women, actually for that commanding officer to know by name almost all of the people. I think, beyond that, it becomes impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. Certainly, you would expect the battalion commander to at least be able to recognise the overwhelming majority of soldiers in his battalion. Whether or not he knows their individual names, he is most likely going to be in a position to where he sees them around the garrison, around the barracks, he is going to recognise them as being soldiers in his battalion?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, certainly, by the time we get to the company level, the company commander is going to know the identity of all soldiers in his company?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think so, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think you would have to agree with me, would you not, that, certainly, the corps commander is not going to be unable to function because he doesn't know the identities of the individual members of the soldiers in the companies all the way down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would certainly agree with you, and I would embellish the point by saying, if the corps commander did know that level of detail, then something would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: The system would not be working as it should.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And he would be focussing on something that a corps commander should not be focussing on?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: That's right, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, of course, we would expect, as you have already said, but just to be clear on this, we would expect the chain of command to work in that scenario, so that, for example, if the battalion commander had a question about the identities of soldiers in his units, he would go to the company commanders for that information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, similarly, if for some reason the brigade commander needed a list of all the soldiers in his brigade, he would go to the battalion commander, who, if need be, would go to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- company commanders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr Mundis, I realise you're not wearing your earphones. The interpreters are asking that you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No problem, will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to wear your earphones; I'm just asking you to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will put them on so that we do not have this problem next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me, again, say to you, sir: We would expect that if that information were needed, the brigade commander could get the names, the identities of the individual soldiers in his battalion by using the chain of command downwards and making inquiries of the brigade commanders -- sorry, the brigade commander would go to the battalion commander, who if need be, would go to the company commanders for that information?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I could agree. If a brigade commander, for some reason, needed to know the identity of all the soldiers in platoon number 33, or whatever, battalion number such-and-such, he would ask that battalion commander, who would then ask the company commander, who would then ask the platoon commander for that information, which would then go all the way up the command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now, sir, to a different topic. You were asked earlier about a situation in which a unit or sub-unit, or perhaps even I believe you said a small number of soldiers, would be in a situation where they answered directly to a political leader. Do you remember that subject, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in describing that situation, or in answering a question from my learned colleague Mr. Robson, you said, on page 52, lines 21 through 25: "As I keep saying, that would be a special arrangement that everybody would understand." My question to, sir, is: What do you mean when you say "everybody would understand"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: If I could give two examples to explain what you mean. There would be or might be circumstances in which specialist forces would be used, and these are often referred to as strategic forces, even a very small number of troops, special force troops; and it's reason they're known as strategic troops is because they carry out tasks of a very high level for which they report back to a very high level; that is to say, if you are in a military system which has special forces, then it would be understood that those forces would have a special chain of command that would not normally go through the standard chamber. The other example for which you would find in a more -- the more regular military hierarchy would be whereby you have troops of a certain level, let's say, a battalion of engineers and, therefore, you would expect that to come under a brigade. Although a battalion, it might be designated divisional level troops and might receive its orders directly from the division and act under the division's command. Again, that would be understood as a specialist arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to return this focus on -- on the smaller unit that is answering directly to a political leader. I would assume, in that situation, we're going to be talking a very senior level political figure who would have such a unit directly subordinated to him or her?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it would be necessarily be a certain individual, but there would be a command level, a very high level command organisation headquarters, in other words, that would be able to issue orders of that sort, and then receive reports directly from it, without going through the normal command chain because they're undertaking, as I said a special strategic task of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear, but, again, I want to focus just for a couple of moments on the situation that you have described, where a unit or a subunit other a very small number of soldiers answers directly to a political authority. When you say "a very high level command organisation headquarters," what type of headquarters are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Well, I think it could go very high. I think it's fairly common knowledge in the UK, for example, that in the past, there have been reports from, again, very small detachments of special forces on certain operations and that those reports would go straight in the highest level of government, where there would be military advice being given, nevertheless it would skip, in other words, most if not all of the levels of the command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Do I understand you to say that it could go to the political level, go beyond the army and go to the political level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, in some of those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, Dr. Cornish, when you say "those reports would go straight in the highest level of government, where there would be military advice being given," what are you talking about? Who is giving this military advice? What are you talking about in that context?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I'm talking there as what I described as the strategic level, where political direction is informed by military advice and part of the decision making process might be to use special forces. I'm talking, really, here about a very specific part of the military structure. Part of the decision might be to use special forces to either conduct a very deep reconnaissance or to be, as happened in the British case, deployed into northern Iraq in the early 1990s to conduct specific operations. The report on success or otherwise of those operations didn't go through a normal military command chain, it was actually -- in my understanding, it was actually radioed straight back to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, sir, in this situation where this information is going to the most senior political leadership of the country, that political leadership is going to be informed or consulted by the most senior levels of the army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that might be considered an ideal type, but that is the ideal type with which I'm most familiar and with which I would, I suppose, be most comfortable. There should be at that level, if civil leadership is making the decision about use of armed force, then it is fundamental, and at least common sense, for that decision making to be informed by military expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn to another topic that was, again, raised this morning, or actually just a few moments ago. Sir, in response to, again, a question from the Presiding Judge, you were asked about the use of booty or captured material as a form of replenishment. Do you remember that sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In response to that question, this is reflected on page 61, lines 7 through 9, you said, "It does happen and will continue to happen. But I would say that in an established military system of the sort with which I'm familiar, that should not happen." But my point is, sir, when you say "established military system of the sort with which you're familiar," what established military system or systems did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: All those where which I've either worked or taught. I could -- the list would include, obviously, the UK, the US, Sweden, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria, and, laterally, the Afghan army. I also, of course, taught many more than I can actually remember, I am afraid to say, during my time at staff college, including lots of African military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But your experience, in effect, has been formed by your professional experience and these projects and things that you have undertaken with respect to predominantly Western military institutions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Predominantly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that your experience with these Western militaries, really, is the basis much of what is in your report, and, certainly, forms your viewpoint as to what is in the report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Certainly, that is the case. Of course, if you're writing document of this sort, then you should always be subjecting yourself to some self-criticism. I think all along, in my work in this area, I have been asking how universalisable - I apologise for that word - to what extent could these principles I have been discussing be considered universal. On the basis of my experience, which has involved working with and teaching and looking at various military systems, and not by any means all of them Western or Western European, I am confident in saying that the principles I have been talking about would not be alien to many more armed forces than just those in Western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that perhaps, or certainly with the excepting of the Afghan army, all of these other armed forces that you mentioned, UK, US, Sweden, Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria, these are highly-developed and well-established military systems?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I have also, over the years, worked and studied other, if you like, less developed and non-Western military systems, ranging from revolutionary guerilla armies to organised guerilla forces. And if you look hard enough, you can find - because as I keep saying, my contention would be that much of this is common sense - you can find parallels, you can find similar principles and codes of conduct, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have no problem, sir, with the concept that the principles are same; but, of course, lesser developed armies might not be in a same position to meet those principles or to put those principles to into practice?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I certainly agree, absolutely, that they would not be able to run themselves at the same tempo and with the same technology as the best developed armies. But the notion of unity of command, for example, would be, as understood, I would contend in any military organisation as it is in the US Army or British Navy or whatever else you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, the aspirations, in terms of fulfilling those principles, or fully meeting those principles, might vary over a wide spectrum depending upon how well established that military force was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think it would. It might take longer or it more complicated or more difficult. There might be different means by which you can achieve the same effect, but that effect of unity and command chain and common purpose and all those things I talk about, I think would still obtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's, then, take a look at this issue of logistics or supply, re-supply, that you were speaking about earlier today, and which actually resulted in the answer that we just been discussing. Obviously, highly developed militaries have highly developed logistical systems; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you comment, sir, on lesser well developed armed forces. Do they have the same level of logistical supply and logistical systems?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: They would have a similar logistical system because there might not be a dependance on, for example, vehicles. There might not be so many artillery guns, and, therefore, such a dependance on artillery ammunition being put through. There might be a narrower requirement and there might be a smaller requirement in certain areas. But somehow there would have to be logistics of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you this because you talked about -- I think you gave a couple of examples. An armed force that uses trucks might face a situation where they would have to requisition fuel on the civilian economy, a situation where armed forces or armies had to, in effect, live off the land, in terms of own nutritional requirements. What about a situation where the armed force or the army was unable to procure weapons and ammunition through the logistical supply chains for whatever reason, how would they do that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be -- I think you're at the point at which the entire system is breaking down. It would seek help from supporting units, supporting countries, whatever else it could. It would have to, but this would be in the most dire circumstance. If the operation is basically running out of fuel and ammunition, then you might argue that it shouldn't have begun in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If that type of weaponry or ammunition was available through the civilian economy, would that be a source for that army to reply itself?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes. I think it could be and it would certainly be considered. I think the example I gave would be coming across a civilian fuel station full of fuel; and if your own system was unable to provide, then it would make sense to requisition that fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the same would go for weaponry or ammunition if it was available on the economy?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: It gets more complicated then, because, you know, what you're looking at there are weapon systems that are, in spite of the fact that one run rifle looks much like the another, the calibres of the ammunition can vary in minute degrees, and that can actually render the weapon unusable. So there is also an issue to do with the dependability of the ammunition and that's why there is a preference, a close preference, to supply standard ammunition to standard weapons within one logistic framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask the same question, where the arm and its ammunition were available from the civilian economy; in other words, you didn't have to use ammunition of a different calibre on a particular weapon, that the replenishment is capable of replenishing you with both the arm and its ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is not something that I confess I'm familiar with. I would have to think closely about it. But I would, also, I think venture the opinion that, in that those circumstances, we come back to an earlier problem, whereby that force, the force in question, were replenishing itself with the most vital means of military activity, which is its ammunition; and, ideally, the command system ought to be able to know, first of all, that it's run out, and, second, that it is replenished. Otherwise, it cannot be really be considered fully part of the overall system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, would your answer be any different, sir, in a combat situation, where, for whatever reason, the army was not able to fully equip and arm a unit? If that unit had recourse to the civilian economy, what steps would that unit take in that situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Then I think, and as I understand it, I believe it's the case that looting and simply stealing what you require is, I think, illegal in international humanitarian law. So there would be some -- should be system whereby the deprived unit would be able to, as I said, requisition what it required, or bought what it required in some way, whether that would be fuel or ammunition or water or food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Cornish, we'll turn again briefly to another subject that was discussed earlier this afternoon, and that has to do with discipline, military discipline. Can you tell us just in the most general way what role discipline -- discipline plays in the armed forces and the fulfilment of military missions?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try. I think what I have been saying is that an individual soldier within a military unit has to be disciplined. They have to be sufficiently well trained and of sufficient motivation and character, if you like, to undertake what I've described this very counter-intuitive activity of being fired at, shot at, and staying where you are, and this requires, I think, would require extraordinary levels of training. There is a requirement then to be disciplined, and military discipline, in my understanding, my interpretation, would be motivated very largely to maintain and ensure that the unit and the individuals remained disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, in fact, would you not agree with me that maintaining good order and discipline is absolutely critical in any military mission?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I would, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn, sir, to some specific things that are contained in your report. I believe you still have that in front of you. Let's talk a little bit about leadership, military leadership, which is section 1. I'd like to draw your attention to particularly the writings of von Clausewitz. Paragraph 7 of your report towards the bottom of page 4 sets forth and continues onto the next page a list of qualities or character qualities which a good military leader should have. Do you see those, sir?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm particularly interested in point A, where you list from von Clausewitz courage. In the second part of that lettered bullet point, if you will, "the courage to accept responsibility, either before the tribunal of some outside power or before the court of one's conscience." Can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I will try to. I believe what Clausewitz means by this is two things; that, first of all, the leader has to be able to do what the soldier does, what I've just described, be able to undertake this enormous stress and danger of being in conflict. He requires that soldierly courage, if I can put it that way. But he also requires a separate, a different level of courage, which is the ability to make a decision, often on the basis of imperfect knowledge, and it then to give instructions on the basis of that judgement, and then also - and perhaps more so - to change that decision when circumstances alter. So it requires, I think what Clausewitz is saying, a -- a extraordinarily, or a -- if you like, a normally courageous person to be extraordinarily capable of taking fast complicated decisions and altering them as time goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What can you say if anything about this aspect of accepting responsibility in terms of being accountable. How important is that for military leaders?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Accountable to what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's take Clausewitz that you have cited to in paragraph 7. When you have quote to him saying "courage to accept responsibility," my question is responsibility for what, responsibility to whom, responsibility -- what exactly -- why did you put this in your report?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Well, the reason I put it in the report was to show that -- I used Sun Tzu and Clausewitz and I think one or two others, was to show that military strategists, military thinkers, have identified there are certain special qualities required of leadership and so I gave them lists of them. That's where that comes from. I think the term "responsibility" in this context really refers to having the strength of character to accept the appointment that you are being offered or instructed to undertake. If you are being given a divisional commander, clearly it makes sense that you should have the confidence and the responsibility to take that on and to know what is involved; and if you don't have that sense of responsibility that it is something that you should and can do, then perhaps you shouldn't take on the appointment in the first place. I think that is what is being got at here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And by accepting this responsibility, is there not a requirement for accountability up the chain of command and, for that matter, down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Yes, I would certainly agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And leadership in this sense, as defined here, as set forth by Clausewitz, this leadership, in terms the responsibility and accountability, sets the tone for the entire command, does it not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think it does, from the bottom through the top. At every level, a leader should be thinking both downwards to those commands and those that they command, and upwards to those who command him. So there is, as you said, sir, a sense of two-track accountability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Cornish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just one point, Dr. Cornish. You were asked about a situation whereby an army does not have sufficient weapons and ammunition, and you were asked whether it might be the case that units may obtain or attempt to obtain ammunition and weapons from a local environment, let's say. Is that the way that an army should work? Should lower level units be able to go off on their own and obtain their own weapons and ammunition, or should it typically be done in a different manner in such extreme situation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I would say that it certainly wouldn't be -- would not be a typical way of doing things. It would not be the preferred way of doing things. The preferred way would be that the military system makes it possible for -- let us say we're talking about an artillery battalion somewhere. The system should make it possible for that artillery battalion to have sufficient fuel and -- ammunition, fuel and water and food to hold itself together and to redeploy itself and move around, and it should then have enough ammunition to undertake the missions it's given. It if it doesn't have enough ammunition, then my sense is that the system begins to decay, to be honest, because logistics isn't simply about providing artillery shells. It's about providing a certain type of artillery shell, which you, the system, can depend upon. You know that this type is able to do certain things at certain ranges with that certain weapon. And if the ammunition is coming from all kinds of other places, then you lose that close understanding of what is possible and, as I said, there might then be other possibilities that the ammunition might actually not work or might prove to be dangerous because of its quality. And then you -- you then end up with your weapon systems grinding to a halt and becoming inoperable. So it would be very, very much the last thing to consider. And, again, I speak from only my limited experience, and my limited experience suggests to me that it would be unlikely for certainly in the -- when we're talking about high-tech advance military systems that they could find the level of replenishment that they would want in a given circumstance. These things, it's no -- I think I'm trying to say, it's no longer simply a matter of providing cannon balls, gunpowder or musket balls. It is much, much more complicated. And my final point is that that whole system, whereby the unit, the artillery battalion, is running out of ammunition and reports the same thing up the chain of command, the chain of command is then functioning or providing another useful function. In that it is providing intelligence about the disposition of your own forces. This battalion of artillery has used up all its ammunition. That means it musts be firing it, and the reason it's firing it is because it is in contact with the enemy, and therefore it needs more. And so you're getting more and more information from what look as though they might be simple straightforward figures of requirement. They actually tell a much, much more important story, and if the supply chain is confined to this -- the known logistics chain, that information can be captured. If logistics is just wherever you can get it, then the information is not organised and is not captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today you mentioned or you spoke about a kind of dialectical relationship between subordinate units and higher units, especially when it comes to having a unit being -- moving or being attached to another battalion. Sorry about the terminology, if I'm not very precise, because I'm a woman, after all. Now this issue of the dialectics, of the exchange of information or suggestions that may come from the lower ranks and going up the chain of command, does that apply also to combat operations, as to how, when and where fighting operations take place in the field? So if there are suggestions or proposals made from a lower unit, are they taken into account?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I think they would be. I didn't use the term dialectical relationship but I think it is a very good one. So thank you for that; I will take note of it. Yes, I think there should be, that exchange of ideas, and I think a mature well-organised and self-confident military command chain would enable precisely that flow to take place. It would require certainly the information that we've all been talking, ammunition and so on, but it would also be sufficiently flexible, such that if a divisional commander, in consultation with his brigade commanders, came up with a plan to do something, and one of the brigade commanders then gave his orders to his battalion commanders, and one of those battalion commanders actually came up with a much better way of doing it, or because of some insight or some observation he could make that nobody else could make, he would then pass that to the brigade commander and the brigade commander would then say to the divisional commander, Here is a new idea. But in the end, after all that exchange of ideas and it is all happening very rapidly, in the end there is authority and there is decision and that someone somewhere, nevertheless, says Thank you for the information, thank you for the ideas, it will be done the following way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still on this issue. If there is a unit tasked with a -- an assault unit, say, tasked with a particular mission which is supposed to operate in the front line, they should break the defence line of the enemy, close combat possibly, if there are opinions expressed by that unit as to how, when and where things should be done, is that going to be taken into account with regard to the assault operation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, I think it could be. What you would expect, though, is that the -- the system, the command chain, the hierarchy, should, if it is working properly, it should already be taking into account what that battalion is able to do, because it has all the information about what the battalion has done, about its personnel, about its ammunition and so on, so there should be a good level of judgment about what could be expected of that battalion. Nevertheless, the battalion commander sees something different, and it would be absolutely essential that he makes that observation clear to his commander and, if necessary, from then up to the next one.
