In the end, though, the battalion commander, having made that observation, having said perhaps, It looks to me as if I won't be able to breakthrough for the following reason, nevertheless, he could conceivably be given an order to go and do precisely that. That's where this authority allies, and that's where this reliance so importantly on military discipline is so essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, in the last instance, you cannot refuse?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last thing - or maybe two - you said that it would be an anathema to skip one wrung in the command chain, and of course the one who -- without the person who suffered this anathema would be informed of what is happening. But if the person who suffered this, that is like the commander that has been skipped. In a system that performs well, how would that commander react? What should his or her reaction be? Can they claim that they have rights? Can they demand some explanation? Can they resign? In your system, I mean, it is just too perfect a system. But in your British Army, how would that work all the same? How would that work? What would they do in your system.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: In the British system, and in many others, if there is a case for removing a unit from the command chain and giving it a special task with special orders so it reports around the command chain, then the commander who has lost a unit would know all about it and would have no objection, because it would have been done properly. He would have received an order that says, One of your battalions is going to be moved over there and is going to doing this and is going to be answering to somebody else for three days or a week. So there's no -- no objection should arise. This is -- can be part of the military function. Our commander knows that and he accepts it. If, nevertheless, it comes to his attention that it has been happening informally, then he would certainly be rather anxious and angry about what had happened. He could require an explanation of the subunit - What are you doing, Why are you doing it, Who told you to do this - and he could then make a representation to his commander to say, This is happening. This is not acceptable, in my view, for my level of command, and it is then the problem for the more senior commander to decide what can be done. In the end, you would expect the system to rectify the fault because it is perceived as a major fault, an anathema, for this to happen, but you could also conceive that the very senior commander might say, It has happened, it shouldn't have happened, but it's happened so let's carry on anyway. There would be procedures and exceptions for representations to be made, but there would be no circumstance I can conceive of in which a brigadier, a commander of a brigade, would say to his divisional commander, I don't like the way things are going and I resign, I'm going home, any more than a private soldier could say, I don't like being fired at, and I'm going home. I don't think it would arise or should arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last point. Do you have any experience in your army or other armies of cases where in wartime in order to defend national territory, voluntary peoples are used and are enrolled, volunteer units who would come also from perhaps their civilian population who would enrol voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Yes, this has happened extensively in military history in the twentieth century; in other words, in more contemporary conflicts. There is nothing unusual about this. In a sense, it has happened a lot, and I'm sure will continue to happen, even to the point at which another very important French expression is used the levee en masse. It is conceivable that the civil population, either en masse or in small units or packets, or even individual people, can want to help. I think my point, though, would be, and I think looking back in -- and this is really just no more than a quick glimpse. I think I would probably expect the commander concerned to receive that help with gratitude but not to rely upon it. So if, let's say, you were conducting an operation in a foreign country somewhere and some of the local people offered to help you with organizing a small defensive position, then you might want to use them, to involve them in the -- in the defence, but you would not probably rely upon them for that defence. You would want to mix them up with your own soldiers and troops so that you could nevertheless be sure that there would be a defence there. Because, in the end, they are not the soldiers that you have trained with, that you can depend upon, that you can expect to act in certain ways. They're very good and brave people, but they're not soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, this system, which is almost perfect which you've described to us will continue to function, or are there exceptions, certain situations which are specific and -- as far as the command and control are concerned about these voluntaries -- volunteers.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I think it does begin to raise all sorts of problems. Would this contingent of people -- the first question would be to establish what they can do, how good are they, and what is their compatibility. Do they all have rifles, or do they have some other weapon. What exactly can they do. Can they interoperate, can they work with other parts of your unit, have they had a sufficient amount of training. Are they going to be joining your organisation, or are they, as we discussed earlier, are they somehow sitting alongside it for as long as they want to be there. So all those difficult questions would arise, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Cornish. It would be a lot easier if we all lived in the perfect world. I asked you at the very beginning of your testimony whether you any legal background, and I did so because I could anticipate that some of the questions that I would have are perhaps of a legal nature. Now, if you're unable to answer some of my questions, then just go ahead and tell me so, because I wouldn't want to you speculate on matters that are outside your expertise. The issue I wish to raise with you is issues of responsibility accountability and, indeed, jurisdiction, over groups which we have been circling around here for the last hour or two. I would say paramilitary groups. So my first question to you is: Do you have any experience or knowledge about how relations are normally handled between regular army troops and paramilitary troops, or units of.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: That would -- I think the larger part of the question would be beyond my experience. What I would say, though, is that it is conceivable that this should happen but there should be a relationship between, as it were, our standard perfect command chain and this non-standard paramilitary organisation, unit, whatever. But there would have to be special efforts put in place for everybody to understand what was going on and why and how this thing fitted in and what it was to do and what it was not to do and so on. So you would expect in those circumstances there to have been a lot of additional effort to make it clear. But, again, I'm going jump into something where I am completely out of my depth, which is to say that we are all, when we are deployed on operational duties, we are all subject to national and international law, and there would be -- a big question I would ask about exactly what would be the status of that organisation, and therefore would it be right and proper for you, the commander, to depend upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What were the efforts that you mentioned were to be made? What sort of efforts are we talking about, just to be clear and -- so we don't misunderstand each other.

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: Let us suppose that our command structure is a division with three brigades and each of those has three battalions, a simple army structure, small army structure, and the divisional commander is informed that a paramilitary organisation, which satisfies all other political and legal requirements, has come along to make a contribution. He would then make it very clear to his brigade commanders precisely who and what that organisation was; and they, in turn, would make it very clear to their subordinate battalion commanders who and what that organisation was, because there has to be, as I have been saying during the morning, there has to be crucially a sense of operational security. There can be no confusion about the disposition of your own forces. There's lots of uncertainty about the enemy and where they are, but there can be as little as possible confusion about your own forces. Because the last things you want to have happen is that in the end a -- a part of your organisation that has been attached to your organisation but that you didn't know about is moving around in front of you and you therefore assume it is an enemy organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me address this issue from a slightly different angle. Why do armies use or seek support of paramilitary units rather than enrolling these units directly into the army? What is the advantage really that you can have of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: If I might answer this question, Your Honour, on the basis of it being a hypothesis. I don't know from my experience that armies with which I'm familiar would do this, other than, I guess, in very, very special circumstances. But I might be able to contribute something usefully from military history, in that in the modern period of industrialised warfare there have been circumstances in which armed forces, armies, have used, if you like, paramilitary forces although they wouldn't have been called that obviously in the early nineteenth century or late eighteenth century, and the idea would have been that these people would provide local knowledge and provide a very intimate understanding of the territory and so on. And so there would be a specific service that they could provide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who, if you know -- or, rather, how would the regular army -- the regular army's military police handle crimes or violations of international humanitarian law committed by paramilitary units; do you know? Do you have any knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge, but I would think this would be a very large-scale challenge, because the system that we're talking about would have a certain capability in military police and military discipline that would be predicated on their being a general disciplined understanding of what to do and what not to do. If, though, our attached paramilitary unit is committing violations of international humanitarian law, then it would, I think, be considered something more than simply military discipline in the field within known parameters and might well be considered beyond the means of a small military police detachment. So I think, and I am speculating, I think it might be considered a very large challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let me move on to another question that I have regarding the responsibility and the accountability of the leadership. That is, the flow of information of which you have already testified at length. I think you explained to us how information is being condensed from its departure at the ground level up through the various levels of command and up -- right up until the main Command Staff. Can you say anything about how this condensation is made? How the selection of information is made on the way up? If you have a combat report, for instance, that begins -- comes from the battalion commander -- even the company commander files a daily combat report an ends it up to the battalion commander who then edits the report and sends the edited report together with the reports that he has received from the other companies up through the -- to the battalion, and the same thing happens therein. What ends finally in the top looks very different from what emanated at the beginning. How is that edition, or the editorial work down? Are there any rules that apply to this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL CORNISH
utterances.text: I don't know so much that there would be rules, but it would be having a close sense of what your next level commander would require. And, again, in the perfect system to which I have been referring, or I prefer to say in terms of the general principles which I have been trying to describe, the -- a mid-level commander would, as part of his training, have been trained in not one but possibly even two levels of command higher up, just in case he has to be given a higher command in time of emergency. So you are trained, or you would be trained, in the sort of information that the next commander would require and so on from you. A low level combat report might involve the number of rounds of shells of artillery that were fired and you might pass that information on to your platoon and company commander and so on. But beyond that, it might not be so useful to burden the command chain with that information, and by the time you get to, let's say, a brigade level, it might be sufficient to say that at that point this unit has taken incoming fire from artillery. And so it would be consolidated and analysed, I guess, as it goes on, because the commander at any level, at whatever level is trying to achieve for his commander what that commander needs, which is situational awareness and so is applying not only judgement about what his subordinates are doing but vicariously -- vicariously is trying to imagine what the commander needs of him and is providing information according.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Dr. Cornish, I see the time is running out. I have one more question, but I wish to consult with my Presiding Officer, or the parties, if you have more questions to put, then I think we might adjourn, but if I only -- if I am the last one to have just one question, then we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In that case, I will postpone my question until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We -- the Court will stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
